title: Tensor Fields and Plates
text:
This article follows a post I’ve found on LinkedIn today, with a naive (better say wrong) use of tensor calculus operators to provide - let’s say, try to provide - a detailed discussion of a Kirchhoff plate subject to transverse load, and the relation of other physical quantities to the spatial derivatives of the out-of-plane displacement field.
All the formulas are collected in the notes about continuum mechanics:

Kirchhoff plate
Timoshenko plate

Pictures are taken from the analytical solution of the hinged rectangular plate with a uniform distributed load, using Fourier basis. This analytical solution may be also an opportunity to discuss Gibbs oscillations close to the boundary.

Bending of a Kirchhoff plate
The transverse displacement \(w(x,y)\) of the a Kirchhoff plate subject to pure bending due to a transverse load \(f_z(x,y)\) is governed by the differential equation
\[D \Delta \Delta w = f_z \ ,\]
supplemented with proper boundary conditions. The fourth-order differential equation is a Laplacian applied twice. As shown in the notes, the right interpretation of the space derivatives of the displacement field \(w(\mathbf{r})\) is:









Figure 1: Out-of-plane displacement \(w(x,y)\)







First derivative and small rotation. The small rotation vector \(\boldsymbol\theta\) is related to the gradient \(\nabla w\)
\[\boldsymbol\theta = - \hat{\mathbf{z}} \times \nabla w \ .\]










Figure 2: Small rotations \(\boldsymbol\theta(x,y)\)







Second derivative and internal moment (tensor). The Laplacian of the displacement field is the opposite of the \(z\)-component of the curl of the infinitesimal rotation
\[\Delta w = - \hat{\mathbf{z}} \cdot \nabla \times \boldsymbol\theta \ .\]
The moment tensor \(\mathbb{M}\) - collecting all the information to get the internal moment acting on the elementary surface with (in-plane) unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{t}}\) as \(\mathbf{M}_{\hat{\mathbf{t}}} = \hat{\mathbf{t}} \cdot \mathbb{M}\) - reads
\[\begin{aligned}
   \mathbb{M}
   & = D \nabla \boldsymbol\theta - m D \nabla^T \boldsymbol\theta = \\
   & = D \begin{bmatrix} \cdot & 1 \\ -1 & \cdot \end{bmatrix} \nabla\nabla w - m D \nabla \nabla w \begin{bmatrix} \cdot & -1 \\ 1 & \cdot \end{bmatrix} \ ,
\end{aligned}\]
and thus the Laplacian of the out-of-plane displacement field is related to the internal moments as
\[\Delta w = \frac{M_{yx} - M_{xy}}{(1+m) D} \ .\]










Figure 3: Moment tensor \(\mathbb{M}(x,y)\)







Third derivative and internal force in \(z\)-direction (vector). The \(z\)-force vector \(\mathbf{F}_z\) collecting all the information to get the internal force in \(z\)-direction acting on the elementary surface with (in-plane) unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{t}}\) as \(F_{z,\hat{\mathbf{t}}} = \hat{\mathbf{t}} \cdot \mathbb{F}_z\) reads
\[\mathbf{F}_z = D \begin{bmatrix} \cdot & 1 \\ -1 & \cdot \end{bmatrix} \Delta \boldsymbol\theta = - D \nabla \Delta w \ .\]










Figure 4: Force vector \(\mathbf{F}(x,y)\)







Fourth derivative and external load. The external distributed load \(f_z\) is proportional to the double Laplacian, as shown in the governing equation,
\[f_z = - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}_z = D \Delta^2 w \ .\]










Figure 5: Fourier approximation of the uniform load \(\sim D \Delta^2 w(x,y) = f_z = \sum_{mn} f_{mn} \sin\left( \frac{m \pi x}{L_x} \right) \sin\left( \frac{n \pi y}{L_y} \right)\), and Laplacian of the out-of-plane displacement, \(\Delta w(x,y)\)






Fourier basis for the hinged plate can’t exactly relresent a uniform load, as the functions of the basis are identically zero on the boundary of the domain. While the approximation improves in most of the domain as the number of used basis functions increases, Gibbs phenomenon occurs at the boundary: sharp oscillations appears in a thin layer close to the domain.

title: About convergence
text:
This post follows the request of proving that
\[\lim_{y \rightarrow 0^+} \frac{y}{\pi} \int_{x=-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{f(x)}{x^2 + y^2} dx = f(0) \ ,\]
for \(f(x)\) continuous and bounded in \(\mathbb{R}\), i.e. that the function \(\frac{y}{\pi (x^2 + y^2)}\) acts as an approximation of the Dirac’s delta as \(y \rightarrow 0^+\).

title: About convergence
section: Method 1: Rigorous Domain Splitting (\(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) / Squeeze Method)
text:
Method 1: Rigorous Domain Splitting (\(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) / Squeeze Method)

1. Algebraic Transformation
Factoring \(y^2\) out of the denominator and using \(d\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = \frac{1}{y} \, dx\):
\[ \frac{y}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{f(x)}{x^2 + y^2} \, dx = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{f(x)}{1 + \left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^2} \, d\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) \]


2. Domain Partitioning
For a fixed parameter \(a > 0\), split the integration domain \((-\infty, +\infty)\) into three regions:
\[ (-\infty, -a] \cup [-a, a] \cup [a, +\infty) \]
Let the corresponding integral be decomposed as:
\[ I(y) = I_1(y) + I_2(y) + I_3(y) \]


3. Evaluating the integrals

3.1 Outer Integrals (\(I_1\) and \(I_3\))
For \(I_3 = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{a}^{+\infty} \frac{f(x)}{1 + (x/y)^2} \, d\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)\), let \(m_3 = \inf_{x \ge a} f(x)\) and \(M_3 = \sup_{x \ge a} f(x)\):
\[ \frac{m_3}{\pi} \int_{a}^{+\infty} \frac{d(x/y)}{1 + (x/y)^2} \le I_3 \le \frac{M_3}{\pi} \int_{a}^{+\infty} \frac{d(x/y)}{1 + (x/y)^2} \]
Evaluating the primitive:
\[ \int_{a}^{+\infty} \frac{d(x/y)}{1 + (x/y)^2} = \left[ \arctan\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) \right]_{x=a}^{x=+\infty} = \frac{\pi}{2} - \arctan\left(\frac{a}{y}\right) \]
Taking the limit as \(y \to 0^+\) (for fixed \(a > 0\)):
\[ \lim_{y \to 0^+} \arctan\left(\frac{a}{y}\right) = \frac{\pi}{2} \implies \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - \arctan\left(\frac{a}{y}\right) \right) \to 0 \]
Thus, \(I_3(y) \to 0\) as \(y \to 0^+\). By symmetric argument, \(I_1(y) \to 0\) as \(y \to 0^+\).


3.2 Middle Integral (\(I_2\)) Around the Origin
For \(I_2 = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-a}^{a} \frac{f(x)}{1 + (x/y)^2} \, d\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)\), let \(m_2(a) = \inf_{x \in [-a, a]} f(x)\) and \(M_2(a) = \sup_{x \in [-a, a]} f(x)\):
\[ \frac{m_2(a)}{\pi} \int_{-a}^{a} \frac{d(x/y)}{1 + (x/y)^2} \le I_2 \le \frac{M_2(a)}{\pi} \int_{-a}^{a} \frac{d(x/y)}{1 + (x/y)^2} \]
Evaluating the primitive:
\[ \int_{-a}^{a} \frac{d(x/y)}{1 + (x/y)^2} = \arctan\left(\frac{a}{y}\right) - \arctan\left(-\frac{a}{y}\right) = 2 \arctan\left(\frac{a}{y}\right) \]
So:
\[ \frac{2 m_2(a)}{\pi} \arctan\left(\frac{a}{y}\right) \le I_2 \le \frac{2 M_2(a)}{\pi} \arctan\left(\frac{a}{y}\right) \]
Taking \(y \to 0^+\) for fixed \(a > 0\), since \(\frac{2}{\pi} \arctan\left(\frac{a}{y}\right) \to 1\):
\[ m_2(a) \le \liminf_{y \to 0^+} I(y) \le \limsup_{y \to 0^+} I(y) \le M_2(a) \]
Finally, taking \(a \to 0^+\), by the continuity of \(f(x)\) at \(x = 0\), we have
\[\lim_{a \to 0^+} m_2(a) = \lim_{a \to 0^+} M_2(a) = f(0)\ , \]
and by the squeeze theorem
\[ \lim_{y \to 0^+} \frac{y}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{f(x)}{x^2 + y^2} \, dx = f(0) \ .\]

section: Method 2: Change of Variables (Dominated Convergence Theorem)

Method 2: Change of Variables (Dominated Convergence Theorem)

1. Substitution
Substitute \(t = \frac{x}{y}\), so \(x = ty\) and \(dx = y \, dt\):
\[ \lim_{y \to 0^+} \frac{y}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{f(x)}{x^2 + y^2} \, dx = \lim_{y \to 0^+} \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{f(ty)}{1 + t^2} \, dt \]


2. Passing the Limit Inside
Assuming \(f\) is bounded (\(|f(x)| \le M\)), the integrand is dominated by an integrable function:
\[ \left| \frac{f(ty)}{1 + t^2} \right| \le \frac{M}{1 + t^2} \in L^1(\mathbb{R}) \]
By Lebesgue’s Dominated Convergence Theorem, we interchange the limit and the integral:
\[ \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \lim_{y \to 0^+} \frac{f(ty)}{1 + t^2} \, dt = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \frac{f(0)}{1 + t^2} \, dt \]


3. Evaluation
\[ = \frac{f(0)}{\pi} \Big[ \arctan(t) \Big]_{-\infty}^{+\infty} = \frac{f(0)}{\pi} \left( \frac{\pi}{2} - \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right) \right) = f(0) \]

text:
Crash introduction to infinitesimal calculus.
This session provides a crash introduction to limits and derivatives. Without going into details of a rigorous definition of the limit of a real function, first section should provide an intuitive idea of the limit, provide some examples of pathological cases, and a bridge to the derivative. The second section should provide an illustration of the geometrical interpretation of the derivative, introducing the definition, and showing the way to evaluate the derivative of some fundamental functions.
A list of the missing steps for a complete understanding of the topics is presented at the end of this section. These steps will be covered in the following sessions.
The interactive html blocks have been designed with the fundamental help of Gemini.

title: Session 3. Crash Introduction to Calculus, Part 1: Limits and Derivatives
text:
Introduction to Limits
See: Matematica: Calcolo infinitesimale: Introduzione al Calcolo: Limiti
Before going into the details of a rigorous definition, this section aims at

providing an intuitive idea of the concept of limit, in 4 cases listed in the SELECT LIMIT CASE dropdown menu. In the finite/finite example for the continuous function \(f(x) = \tfrac{x^2-1}{2}\), taking the limit for \(x \rightarrow 2\) just means evaluating the function \(f(x)\) for \(x = 2\), and thus \(\lim_{x\rightarrow 2} f(x) = f(2) = \tfrac{3}{2}\)
showing some pathological cases: a function “with jumps” (a discontinuous function), an “increasingly fast” oscillating function (\(\sin(1/x)\) for \(x \rightarrow 0\))
presenting an example of indeterminate form \(\tfrac{0}{0}\). The function \(f(x) = \tfrac{x^2-4}{x-2}\) is the ratio of two polynomial functions whose values are zero for \(x=2\). The existence conditions for \(f(x)\) read \(x \ne 2\), otherwise the denominator becomes equal to zero (and we know that’s not possible to divide by zero). Anyway, the limit operation allows to study the behavior of the function as \(x\) approaches \(2\). Since \(x^2-4 = (x-2)(x+2)\), for all the \(x \ne 2\) the function \(f(x) = \tfrac{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+2)}{\cancel{x-2}}\) is equivalent to \(x+2\). Now, \(x+2\) is a continuous function - as in the first bullet of this item list - that gives no issues at all when evaluated for \(x = 2\).
\[\lim_{x \rightarrow 2} \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = \lim_{x \rightarrow 2} \left( x + 2 \right) = 4  \ .\]

title: Session 3. Crash Introduction to Calculus, Part 1: Limits and Derivatives
text:
Introduction to Derivatives
See: Matematica: Calcolo infinitesimale: Derivata
A geometrical interpretation is presented first, then the definition is provided along with the fundamental derivatives.

Geometrical Interpretation
In the previous sessions, we tried to get familiar with real functions and their graph. Now, we provide the geometrical interpretation of the derivative \(f'(x)\) of a function \(f(x)\). Given a function \(f(x)\), the function \(f'(x)\) provides the slope of the tangent line to the graph of the function in point \((x, f(x))\).


  
  



Definition
The derivative \(f'(x)\) of function \(f(x)\), evaluated for the generic value \(x\) of the independent variable can be interpreted as the slope of the tangent line in \((x, f(x))\). Using the interactive tab, this is equivalent to - for a given point \(A \equiv (x, f(x))\), i.e. for a given value \(x\) - to make the point \(B \equiv ( x + \Delta x, f(x+\Delta x))\) approach the point \(A\), i.e. to make \(\Delta x \rightarrow 0\). As the slope of the secant line through \(A\) and \(B\) is defined as the incremental ratio
\[m_{AB}^{sec} = \frac{y_B - y_A}{x_B-x_A} =  \frac{f(x+\Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} \ ,\]
the slope of the tangent line in \(A\) is just the limit for \(\Delta x \rightarrow 0\) of the incremental ratio,
\[m_{A}^{tan} = \lim_{\Delta x \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+\Delta x) - f(x)}{\Delta x} =: f'(x) \ .\]
As the point \(B\) approaches \(A\), the the secant approaches the tangent line (if there’s a tangent line in \(A\), and thus if the derivative in \(x\) exists).


Derivative of fundamental functions
See: Matematica: Calcolo infinitesimale: Derivata: Derivata delle funzioni fondamentali

Let’s mainly focus on the polynomial functions here.

Computation of your first derivatives, using the definition. Just focus on the polynomial functions (Exercise 25.1, n.1., 2.) and have fun with the square root n.6 (Hint: rationalization after inserting the function \(\sqrt{x}\) in the definiton), and the rational function n.7 (Hint: common denominator)

Next steps
Integrals. Given the fundamental theorem of calculus, the integral is the opposite operation of the derivative. We need to understand that, and take all the steps taken with derivatives backwards: integrals of fundamental functions, rules of integration,…
Ordinary differential equations. Lots of systems of interest are governed by differential equations, especially in physics, classical mechanics and engineering. A differential equation is nothing but an equation containing a unknown function and its derivatives. We’ll introduce and solve the simplest ones, that nonetheless can be used as the mathematical model of lots of systems. Just as an example,

under some circumstances, the temperature of a body \(T(t)\) with mass \(m\), heat capacity \(C\), in an environment with temperature \(T_e(t)\) and that can exchange heat with the body, is governed by the differential equation
\[m C T'(t) + h T(t) = h T_e(t) \ .\]
Here, with all the other parameters and functions given, \(T(t)\) is the unknown of the problem.
under some circumstances, the position of a mass connected to the ground with a spring and a damper, and subject to an external force \(F_e(t)\) is governed by the differential equation
\[m x''(t) + c x'(t) + k x(t) = F_e(t) \ .\]
Here, with all the other parameters and functions given, \(x(t)\) is the unknown of the problem.

As we all learned how to solve algebraic equations, we’ll learn how to solve the simplest ordinary differential equations.

section: The idea behind the general solution of linear ODEs with constant coefficients
text:
The idea behind the general solution of linear ODEs with constant coefficients

Free solution
The free evolution of a system governed by a \(n^{th}\)-order linear ODE with constant coefficients, is the solution of the homogeneous (unforced, free) equation
\[y^{(n)}(t) + a_{n-1} y^{(n-1)}(t) + a_1 y'(t) + a_0 y(t) = 0 \ .\]
is a linear combination of (in general, complex) \(n\) exponential functions, \(e^{s_k t}\), for \(k=1:n\). In order to find all the values of the \(s_k\)s, the solution is assumed to be \(y(t) = C e^{s t}\). Its first derivative reads \(y'(t) = C s e^{st} = s y(t)\), its second derivative reads \(y''(t) = s^2 e^{st} = s^2 y(t)\), and so on. Replacing the expression of the derivatives in the homogeneous equation, and collecting and removing the never-zero factor \(y(t)\), an algebraic equation appears,
\[s^n + a_{n-1} s^{n-1} + \dots a_1 s + a_0 = 0 \ ,\]
whose \(n\) solutions (it’s a polynomial equation of degree \(n\), it has \(n\) complex solutions) are the values of the \(s_k\). The homogenoeus solution of the equation is thus a linear combination of the exponential functions,
\[y_{homo}(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} C_k e^{s_k t} \ .\]

1 Model

1.1 Governing equations
Shallow water equations. Conservative form of the equations
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \zeta + \nabla \cdot ( \zeta \mathbf{u} ) = 0 \\
  & \partial_t ( \zeta \mathbf{u} ) + \nabla \cdot \left( \zeta \mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u} + \frac{g \zeta^2}{2} \mathbb{I} \right) = \text{variable depth} + \text{non inertial + tidal + dissipation} \ ,
\end{aligned}\right.\]
while convective form reads
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \zeta + \nabla \cdot ( \zeta \mathbf{u} ) = 0 \\
  & \zeta \partial_t  \mathbf{u} + \zeta \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} + g \zeta \nabla \zeta = \text{variable depth} + \text{non inertial + tidal + dissipation}
\end{aligned}\right.\]
or, dividing the momentum equation by \(\zeta\)
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \zeta + \nabla \cdot ( \zeta \mathbf{u} ) = 0 \\
  & \partial_t  \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u} + g \nabla \zeta = \text{variable depth} + \text{non inertial + tidal + dissipation}
\end{aligned}\right.\]
The sum of Moon gravitational pull and non-inertial force per unit-mass, with constant angular velocity of the non-inertial reference frame w.r.t. the inertial ref.frame \(\boldsymbol\omega_{1/0}\) s.t. \(\boldsymbol\alpha_{1/0} = \mathbf{0}\), reads
\[-\mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{P/O} - 2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v}^{(1)} - \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times ({\rm P}-{\rm Q}) \ .\]
Using spherical coordinates \(\boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} = \Omega_{1/0} \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), \(\mathbf{v}^{(1)} = v_{\varphi}\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi} + v_{\theta}\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}\), \({\rm P}-{\rm Q} = a \hat{\mathbf{R}}\),

tidal forces
…
centrifugal acceleration
\[\boldsymbol\omega \times \boldsymbol\omega \times (P-Q) = \Omega^2 a \, \hat{\mathbf{z}} \sin \varphi \times \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} = - \Omega^2 a \sin \varphi \hat{\boldsymbol\rho} = \Omega^2 a \left( - \sin^2 \varphi \, \hat{\mathbf{R}} - \sin \varphi \cos \varphi \, \hat{\boldsymbol\varphi} \right) \]
Coriolis force (divided by \(2\))
\[\boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v}^{(1)} = \Omega \hat{\mathbf{z}} \times ( v_{\varphi}\hat{\boldsymbol\varphi} + v_{\theta}\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) = \Omega v_\varphi \cos \varphi \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} - \Omega v_\theta \hat{\boldsymbol\rho} =  \Omega v_\varphi \cos \varphi \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} - \Omega v_\theta \left( \sin \varphi \, \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \cos \varphi \, \hat{\boldsymbol\varphi} \right) \ ,\]
i.e., using lat \(\phi = \frac{\pi}{2} - \varphi\),
\[2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v}^{(1)} = - 2 \Omega v_\theta \cos \phi \, \hat{\mathbf{R}} + 2 \Omega \, \sin \phi \left( -v_\theta \hat{\boldsymbol\varphi} + v_\varphi \hat{\boldsymbol\theta} \right) \]

Steady reference state.

Centrifugal force is constant in the non-inertial reference frame, so it only acts on the steady reference state and not in the unsteady linearized equations around that.
Linearized equations around the reference state \(\left.\left(\zeta, \mathbf{u}\right)\right|_{\rm ref} = (\zeta_0(\mathbf{r}), \mathbf{0})\)
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \zeta' + \nabla \cdot \left( \zeta_0  \mathbf{u}'  \right) = 0 \\
  & \partial_t \mathbf{u}' + g \nabla \zeta' = -2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{u}' - r \mathbf{u}' + \text{tidal forces}
\end{aligned}\right.\]

i.c + b.c.

Frequency domain. Frequency response of the system is studied in frequency domain, with Fourier transform of the functions, \(\hat{f}(\mathbf{r}, \omega) := \mathcal{F}\{ f(\mathbf{r}, t) \}(\omega)\), and the linearized equations for \(\left( \hat{\zeta}, \hat{\mathbf{u}} \right)(\mathbf{r}, \omega)\),
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & i \omega \hat{\zeta} + \nabla \cdot \left( \zeta_0  \hat{\mathbf{u}} \right) = 0 \\
  & i \omega \hat{\mathbf{u}} + g \nabla \hat{\zeta} + 2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \hat{\mathbf{u}} + r \hat{\mathbf{u}} = \hat{\mathbf{g}}_{\rm tidal}(\omega) \ .
\end{aligned}\right.\]

i.c + b.c.

Assumptions.

Mainly the reason why tidal forces are neglected and replaced by a prescribe level of the sea at the open boundary of the domain

\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}

\end{aligned} \right.\]
or using latitude \(\phi = \frac{\pi}{2} - \varphi\), so that \(v := v_\phi = - \varphi\), \(\partial_\varphi = - \partial_\phi\), \(g_{\phi} = - g_{\varphi}\),
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}

\end{aligned} \right.\]

2 Numerical methods

2.1 From continuous to discrete equations - FVM/FDM
The solver implemented here can be interpreted both as a FV or a FD solver… The discrete counterpart of the continuous equations
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & i \omega \hat{\zeta} + \frac{1}{\cos \phi} \left[ \partial_\theta ( \zeta_0 \hat{v}_\theta ) + \partial_\phi( \zeta_0 \hat{v}_\phi \cos \phi ) \right] = 0 \\
  & i \omega \hat{v}_\theta + \frac{g}{a \cos \phi} \partial_\theta  \hat{\zeta} + r \hat{v}_\theta - 2 \Omega \cos \phi \hat{v}_\phi = \hat{g}_{\theta, \rm tidal} \\
  & i \omega \hat{v}_\phi + \frac{g}{a             } \partial_\phi \hat{\zeta} + r \hat{v}_\phi + 2 \Omega \cos \phi \hat{v}_\theta = \hat{g}_{\phi, \rm tidal}
\end{aligned} \right.\]
are:

Continuity equation
\[0 = i \omega \hat{\zeta}_{i,j} \underbrace{ \Delta \widetilde{V}_{i,j} \cos \phi_{i,j} }_{\Delta V_{i,j}} - \left.\left( \zeta_0 \hat{u} \Delta S_{\theta} \right)\right|_{i-\frac{1}{2},j} + \left.\left( \zeta_0 \hat{u} \Delta S_{\theta} \right)\right|_{i+\frac{1}{2},j} - \left.\left( \zeta_0 \hat{v} \Delta S_{\phi} \right)\right|_{i,j-\frac{1}{2}} + \left.\left( \zeta_0 \hat{u} \Delta S_{\phi} \right)\right|_{i,j+\frac{1}{2}} \ ,\]






NoteDetails





being

\(\Delta \widetilde{V}_{i,j} = a^2 \Delta \theta \Delta \phi\) the area of the cell in the coordinate space \((\theta, \phi)\), so that the area on the spherical surface is \(\Delta V_{i,j} = \Delta \widetilde{V}_{i,j} \cos \phi_{i,j}\),
\(\Delta S^\theta = a \Delta \phi\) the size of the west/east faces
\(\Delta S^\phi = a \cos \phi_{n,s} \Delta \theta\) the size of the north/south faces, being \(\varphi_{n,s}\) the value of \(\varphi\) at the north/south faces respectively

In a structured grid, west/east faces of the same cell have the same \(\Delta \phi\), north/south faces of the same cell have the same \(\Delta \theta\).
In the staggered grid solver: * the reference depth at faces are interpolated from cell-centered values * the required components of the velocity are defined on the faces.
Remarks. * Metric contributions already appears in the differential form of the equations * the \(\cos \phi\) contribution appearing in \(\Delta V = \cos \phi \, \Delta \theta \Delta \phi\) is at the denominator of the flux terms (of the divergence \(\nabla \cdot (\zeta_0  \mathbf{u})\)) * the \(\cos \phi\) contribution appearing in \(\Delta S^{\phi} = \cos \phi \, \Delta \phi\) multiplies \(\zeta_0 v\) * The elementary area on the spherical surface is consistent with the results of differential geometry, \(d A = a^2 \sin \varphi \, d \theta d \varphi\)
Thus, dividing by \(\Delta V_{i,j}\) the scaled contributions of the surfaces are
\[\begin{aligned}
  \frac{\Delta S^{\theta}_{i \mp \frac{1}{2},j}}{\Delta V_{i,j}} & = \frac{1}{a  \cos \phi_{i,j} \, \Delta \theta_{i,j}} \\
  \frac{\Delta S^{\phi}_{i \mp \frac{1}{2},j}}{\Delta V_{i,j}} & = \frac{\cos \phi_{s,n}}{a  \cos \phi_{i,j} \, \Delta \phi_{i,j}} \\
\end{aligned}\]





Momentum equation: \(\theta\)-component
\[\left( i \omega \hat{u}_{i+\frac{1}{2},j} + r \hat{u}_{i+\frac{1}{2},j} - 2 \Omega \cos \phi_{i,j} \, \text{Avg}\{ v_{i+\frac{1}{2}, j } \} \right) \underbrace{ \Delta \widetilde{V}_{i+\frac{1}{2},j} \cos \phi_{i,j} }_{\Delta V_{i+\frac{1}{2}, j} } - \left.\left( \frac{g}{a} \hat{\zeta} \Delta S_{\theta} \right)\right|_{i,j} + \left.\left(  \frac{g}{a} \hat{\zeta} \Delta S_{\theta} \right)\right|_{i+1,j} = \dots \ ,\]


Momentum equation: \(\phi\)-component
\[\left( i \omega \hat{v}_{i,j+\frac{1}{2}} + r \hat{u}_{i,j+\frac{1}{2}} - 2 \Omega \cos \phi_{i,j+\frac{1}{2}} \, \text{Avg}\{ u_{i, j+\frac{1}{2} } \} \right) \Delta \widetilde{V}_{i,j+\frac{1}{2}} - \left.\left( \frac{g}{a} \hat{\zeta} \Delta \widetilde{S}_{\phi} \right)\right|_{i,j} + \left.\left(  \frac{g}{a} \hat{\zeta} \Delta \widetilde{S}_{\phi} \right)\right|_{i+1,j} = \dots \ ,\]
with
\[\frac{\Delta \widetilde{S}_{\phi}}{ \Delta \widetilde{V}} = \frac{a \Delta \theta}{a^2 \Delta \phi \Delta \theta} = \frac{1}{a \Delta \phi} \ .\]



2.2 Characteristics of the hyperbolic problem and flux boundary conditions (e.g. for Finite Volume Methods)






NoteDetails of the eigen-structure of the linear hyperbolic system





n-dimensional linearized shallow water equations.
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \zeta' + \nabla \cdot ( \zeta_0 \mathbf{u}' ) = 0 \\
  & \partial_t ( \zeta_0 \mathbf{u}' ) + \nabla \cdot \left( g \zeta_0 \zeta' \mathbb{I} \right) = \text{variable depth} + \text{non inertial + tidal + dissipation} \ ,
\end{aligned}\right.\]
1-dimensional linearized shallow water equations.
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \partial_t \zeta' + \partial_x ( \zeta_0 u' ) = 0 \\
  & \partial_t ( \zeta_0 u' ) + \partial_x \left( g \zeta_0 \zeta' \right) = \text{variable depth} + \text{non inertial + tidal + dissipation} \ ,
\end{aligned}\right.\]
Conservative form
\[
\partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \zeta' \\ \zeta_0 u' \end{bmatrix} + \partial_x \begin{bmatrix} \zeta_0 u' \\ g \zeta_0 \zeta' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \text{non inertial + tidal + dissipation} \end{bmatrix}
\]
Convective form
\[
\partial_t \begin{bmatrix} \zeta' \\ \zeta_0 u' \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ g \zeta_0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \partial_x \begin{bmatrix} \zeta' \\ \zeta_0 u' \end{bmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \partial_x( g \zeta_0 ) \, \zeta' \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \text{non inertial + tidal + dissipation} \end{bmatrix}
\]
The characteristic velocities of the linearized hyperbolic problem are the eigenvalues of the advection matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), here
\[0 = \left| \mathbf{A} - s_{1,2} \mathbf{I} \right| = s^2 - g\zeta_0 \quad \rightarrow \quad s_{1,2} = \mp \sqrt{g \zeta_0} =: \mp c_0 \ ,\]
with corresponding right and left eigenvectors collected as the columns of matrices \(\mathbf{R}\) and \(\mathbf{L}\),
\[\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{R} = \begin{bmatrix} \zeta_0 & \zeta_0 \\ \zeta_0 c_0 & - \zeta_0 c_0 \end{bmatrix}
  \quad , \quad
  \mathbf{L} = \mathbf{R}^{-1} = \frac{1}{2 \zeta_0 c_0} \begin{bmatrix} -c_0 & -1 \\ - c_0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}\]
Since the 2 characteristic velocities have opposite sign, in every point of the domain there’s a family of characteristics moving to the right and one family moving to the left. At the boundaries of the domain, there’s always a familiy of characteristics leaving the domain, and one family entering the domain.
This observation is used in the implementation of boundary conditions for finite volume methods.

2.4 Frequency response
The discrete version of the linearized system in Fourier domain can be formally written as
\[\left( i \omega \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A}(\overline{\mathbf{u}}) \right) \hat{\mathbf{u}}(\omega) = \hat{\mathbf{f}}(\omega) \ ,\]
being \(\overline{\mathbf{u}}\) the reference state, and \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{f}}\) the Fourier transform of the state and the forcing acting on the linearized system. This is the usual representation of a MIMO system with \((i \omega \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A})^{-1}\) as the matrix of the transfer functions.

"""
Level 3 - regional tide model of an Adriatic-like basin  (Colab / Plotly)
=========================================================================
Linear, frequency-domain solution of the rotating shallow-water (Laplace tidal) equations
on a masked spherical C-grid, driven through the open boundary at the Otranto strait.

MODEL ASSUMPTIONS
  1. Linearised depth-averaged shallow water on the rotating sphere (f-term kept, no advection,
     no stratification -> no internal tides), hydrostatic, single layer.
  2. One constituent at a time (M2, S2, K1, O1): fields ~ Re[ Z(x,y) exp(i sigma t) ].
  3. Linearised quadratic bottom drag  r = Cd*U0/h  (floor R_MIN); U0 is the one tuning knob.
  4. Closed coasts: no normal flow (free slip). No wetting/drying, rivers, islands, tidal flats.
  5. Local astronomical forcing neglected inside the basin (order 1 cm); the tide is driven by
     the open boundary. No atmosphere: no wind, no pressure -> no storm surge (e.g. no 'acqua alta'
     from sirocco). No self-attraction/loading. Constant Earth radius, spherical geometry.
  6. Bathymetry: IDEALISED (default) = hand-digitised coastline (islands omitted, +-10-20 km) with a
     schematic depth profile; or ETOPO 2022 (USE_REAL_BATHYMETRY=True, needs internet, see below).

BOUNDARY CONDITIONS
  * Coasts / domain edges: u.n = 0.
  * Open boundary (southern edge, Ionian side, lon in OPEN_LON): Flather radiation condition
        u_out = sqrt(g/h) * (zeta - zeta_ext),
    zeta_ext = uniform complex external level (the Ionian sea as an oscillating water level).
    zeta is extrapolated to the boundary face with 2nd-order accuracy; waves leaving the basin
    pass through. zeta_ext is CHOSEN (one complex number per constituent, by linearity) so that the
    model reproduces the published Otranto gauge amplitude and phase (as a 30 km average around the
    gauge, to be robust against coastal gradients; CALIBRATE_FORCING=True; False uses the gauge values directly as zeta_ext). All other stations
    are then predictions. Tuned quantities: this forcing and the drag U0; the depth profile is
    calibrated to the real mean depth (~250 m), not to tides.

Time convention: zeta = Re[Z exp(i sigma t)] = |Z| cos(sigma t - g),  g = -arg Z = phase lag.

Observed constants (cm, degrees; phases relative to 15E) = Table 1 of
Janekovic & Kuzmic (2005), Ann. Geophys. 23, 3207 - transcribed with a text-extraction tool:
CHECK AGAINST THE PAPER before quoting them.

# ═══════════════════════════ geometry / bathymetry ═══════════════════════════
def make_grid(res):
    nx = int(round((LON1 - LON0)/res))
    ny = int(round((LAT1 - LAT0)/res))
    return nx, ny, LON0 + (np.arange(nx) + 0.5)*res, LAT0 + (np.arange(ny) + 0.5)*res


def in_polygon(px, py, poly):
    inside = np.zeros(px.shape, bool)
    x, y = poly[:, 0], poly[:, 1]
    j = len(poly) - 1
    for i in range(len(poly)):
        cond = ((y[i] > py) != (y[j] > py)) & (px < (x[j] - x[i])*(py - y[i])/(y[j] - y[i] + 1e-300) + x[i])
        inside ^= cond
        j = i
    return inside


def synthetic_bathymetry(res):
    nx, ny, lon_c, lat_c = make_grid(res)
    LON, LAT = np.meshgrid(lon_c, lat_c)
    wet = in_polygon(LON, LAT, COAST)
    hmax = np.interp(LAT, HP_LAT, HP_H)
    dkm = ndimage.distance_transform_edt(wet, sampling=(111.2*res, 111.2*res*np.cos(np.radians(43.0))))
    return wet, hmax*np.tanh(dkm/SHELF_KM)


ETOPO = None   # cache: (lat, lon, z) arrays


def load_etopo(timeout=90):
    """ETOPO 2022 (15 arc-s) from NOAA ERDDAP, thinned to 1 arc-min; z<0 below sea level.
    Tries a few mirrors/orderings; returns None on failure (script falls back to synthetic)."""
    cands = [
        ("https://coastwatch.pfeg.noaa.gov/erddap/griddap/ETOPO_2022_v1_15s.csv?z[(%g):4:(%g)][(%g):4:(%g)]", (LAT0, LAT1, LON0, LON1)),
        ("https://coastwatch.pfeg.noaa.gov/erddap/griddap/ETOPO_2022_v1_15s.csv?z[(%g):4:(%g)][(%g):4:(%g)]", (LAT1, LAT0, LON0, LON1)),
        ("https://coastwatch.pfeg.noaa.gov/erddap/griddap/etopo180.csv?altitude[(%g):(%g)][(%g):(%g)]", (LAT0, LAT1, LON0, LON1)),
    ]
    for tmpl, args in cands:
        try:
            txt = urllib.request.urlopen(tmpl % args, timeout=timeout).read().decode()
            arr = np.loadtxt(io.StringIO(txt), delimiter=",", skiprows=2)     # lat, lon, z  (row 2 = units)
            if arr.ndim == 2 and arr.shape[0] > 1000 and np.isfinite(arr[:, 2]).all():
                return arr[:, 0], arr[:, 1], arr[:, 2]
        except Exception as e:
            print("   ETOPO request failed (%s): %s" % (tmpl.split("?")[0].split("/")[-1], str(e)[:80]))
    return None


def etopo_bathymetry(res):
    lat, lon, z = ETOPO
    nx, ny, lon_c, lat_c = make_grid(res)
    ji = np.floor((lat - LAT0)/res).astype(int)
    ii = np.floor((lon - LON0)/res).astype(int)
    ok = (ji >= 0) & (ji < ny) & (ii >= 0) & (ii < nx)
    cnt, sea, dep = np.zeros((ny, nx)), np.zeros((ny, nx)), np.zeros((ny, nx))
    np.add.at(cnt, (ji[ok], ii[ok]), 1.0)
    s = ok & (z < 0)
    np.add.at(sea, (ji[s], ii[s]), 1.0)
    np.add.at(dep, (ji[s], ii[s]), -z[s])
    return sea > 0.5*np.maximum(cnt, 1), dep/np.maximum(sea, 1.0)


def make_basin(res):
    nx, ny, lon_c, lat_c = make_grid(res)
    wet, h = etopo_bathymetry(res) if ETOPO is not None else synthetic_bathymetry(res)
    openm = wet[0] & (lon_c >= OPEN_LON[0]) & (lon_c <= OPEN_LON[1])
    lab, _ = ndimage.label(wet)                                  # keep water connected to the open boundary
    keep = np.unique(lab[0][openm]); keep = keep[keep > 0]
    wet = np.isin(lab, keep)
    H = np.where(wet, np.maximum(h, MIN_DEPTH), 0.0)
    return make_B(wet, H, res, lon_c, lat_c, wet[0] & openm)


def make_B(wet, H, res, lon_c, lat_c, openm):
    R = np.where(wet, np.maximum(CD*U0/np.maximum(H, MIN_DEPTH), R_MIN), 0.0)
    return dict(wet=wet, H=H, res=res, lon_c=lon_c, lat_c=lat_c, open=openm, R=R)


# ═══════════════════════════ solver ═══════════════════════════
def solve_tide(B, sigma, Zext, coriolis=True):
    """Complex zeta on the grid for one angular frequency sigma (time dependence exp(i sigma t))."""
    wet, H, openm, Rf = B["wet"], B["H"], B["open"], B["R"]
    ny, nx = wet.shape
    d = np.radians(B["res"])
    #> Latitude at cell center
    latc = np.radians(B["lat_c"])[:, None]*np.ones((1, nx))
    #> Cosine of the latitude evaluated at cell center, and on north/south faces
    cosc, cosn, coss = np.cos(latc), np.cos(latc + d/2), np.cos(latc - d/2)
    Zext = np.broadcast_to(np.asarray(Zext, complex), (nx,))
    cor = 1.0 if coriolis else 0.0

    # unknown numbering: zeta (cells) | u (east faces) | v (north faces) | vb (open-boundary faces)
    nz = int(wet.sum())
    zi = -np.ones((ny, nx), int); zi[wet] = np.arange(nz)
    ue = wet[:, :-1] & wet[:, 1:]
    ui = -np.ones((ny, nx - 1), int); ui[ue] = nz + np.arange(ue.sum())
    nu = int(ue.sum())
    ve = wet[:-1, :] & wet[1:, :]
    vi = -np.ones((ny - 1, nx), int); vi[ve] = nz + nu + np.arange(ve.sum())
    nv = int(ve.sum())
    bi = -np.ones(nx, int); bi[openm] = nz + nu + nv + np.arange(openm.sum())
    nb = int(openm.sum())
    N = nz + nu + nv + nb
    UE = -np.ones((ny, nx), int); UE[:, :-1] = ui          # east / west faces of every cell
    UW = -np.ones((ny, nx), int); UW[:, 1:] = ui
    VN = -np.ones((ny, nx), int); VN[:-1] = vi             # north / south faces of every cell
    VS = -np.ones((ny, nx), int); VS[1:] = vi; VS[0] = bi

    #> Avg of ref depth and dissipation coeff. From cell center to faces
    #> u defined on west/east faces. hu depth on the face, avg of the depth in left/right cells;
    #> v defined on north/south faces. hv depth on the face, avg of the depth in north/south cells;
    hu = 0.5*(H[:, :-1] + H[:, 1:]); ru = 0.5*(Rf[:, :-1] + Rf[:, 1:])
    hv = 0.5*(H[:-1] + H[1:]); rv = 0.5*(Rf[:-1] + Rf[1:])
    rr, cc, vv = [], [], []

    def add(r, c, v):
        """
        Fill the elements of a sparse matrix with the given values.
        r: row indices
        c: column indices
        v: values

        vectors rr, cc, vv initialized outside the function
        """
        c = np.asarray(c)
        v = np.broadcast_to(np.asarray(v, complex), c.shape)
        r = np.broadcast_to(np.asarray(r), c.shape)

        m = c >= 0 # why this check?

        rr.append(r[m]);  cc.append(c[m]);  vv.append(v[m])

    #> Building matrices of the linear system, on the STAGGERED grid
    #> Eq1., continuity: i sigma zeta + (1/(a cos)) [ d(h u)/dlon + d(h v cos)/dlat ] = 0
    # continuity equation for cell i has the same index as z for cell i
    #> Volume contributions: i*sigma
    jj, ii = np.nonzero(wet)
    add(zi[jj, ii], zi[jj, ii], 1j*sigma)
    #> Flux contributions
    # from surfaces orthogonal to theta
    jj, ii = np.nonzero(ue)
    add(zi[jj, ii], ui[jj, ii], hu[jj, ii]/(A_E*cosc[jj, ii]*d))          # contribution to the left cell
    add(zi[jj, ii + 1], ui[jj, ii], -hu[jj, ii]/(A_E*cosc[jj, ii + 1]*d)) # contribution to the right cell
    # from surfaces orthogonal to varphi
    jj, ii = np.nonzero(ve)
    add(zi[jj, ii], vi[jj, ii], cosn[jj, ii]*hv[jj, ii]/(A_E*cosc[jj, ii]*d))
    add(zi[jj + 1, ii], vi[jj, ii], -cosn[jj, ii]*hv[jj, ii]/(A_E*cosc[jj + 1, ii]*d))
    #> Boundary contributions
    ib = np.nonzero(openm)[0]
    add(zi[0, ib], bi[ib], -coss[0, ib]*H[0, ib]/(A_E*cosc[0, ib]*d))

    # zonal momentum: (i sigma + r) u - f vbar + g/(a cos) dzeta/dlon = 0
    jj, ii = np.nonzero(ue)
    row = ui[jj, ii]
    add(row, row, 1j*sigma + ru[jj, ii])
    coef = g_acc/(A_E*cosc[jj, ii]*d)
    add(row, zi[jj, ii + 1], coef)
    add(row, zi[jj, ii], -coef)
    #> Coriolis force: u, v variables are not co-located, but in a grid of points
    # shifted of dx/2, dy/2 in x- and y-directions. The x component of the momentum
    # equation has u-component of the velocity as dynamic variable; Coriolis force
    # in x-mom equation comes from v-component of the velocity; thus, approximation
    # of v using the values in the "neighboring" 4-points is required. Here each
    # of the 4 values is weighted by 1/4
    # phi in Coriolis force is the same as the phi used in the cell-centered grid
    # used for zeta
    fu = cor*2*OMEGA*np.sin(latc[jj, ii])
    # avg of the neighboring values of v
    for nb_ in (VN[jj, ii], VN[jj, ii + 1], VS[jj, ii], VS[jj, ii + 1]):
        add(row, nb_, -0.25*fu)

    # meridional momentum: (i sigma + r) v + f ubar + g/a dzeta/dlat = 0
    jj, ii = np.nonzero(ve)
    row = vi[jj, ii]
    add(row, row, 1j*sigma + rv[jj, ii])
    add(row, zi[jj + 1, ii], g_acc/(A_E*d))
    add(row, zi[jj, ii], -g_acc/(A_E*d))
    #> Coriolis force contribution: see the comment above in the x-comp of the 
    # momentum equation
    # phi in Coriolis force is shifted in the latitude direction w.r.t. the cell-centered grid
    # used for zeta and u
    fv = cor*2*OMEGA*np.sin(latc[jj, ii] + d/2)
    # avg of the neighboring values of u
    for nb_ in (UW[jj, ii], UE[jj, ii], UW[jj + 1, ii], UE[jj + 1, ii]):
        add(row, nb_, 0.25*fv)

    # open boundary (Flather): vb + c zeta_b = c Zext,  c = sqrt(g/h), zeta_b = 1.5 zeta0 - 0.5 zeta1
    c = np.sqrt(g_acc/H[0, ib])
    add(bi[ib], bi[ib], 1.0)
    two = wet[1, ib] if ny > 1 else np.zeros(ib.size, bool)
    add(bi[ib], zi[0, ib], np.where(two, 1.5*c, c))
    add(bi[ib], np.where(two, zi[1, ib], -1), -0.5*c)
    rhs = np.zeros(N, complex)
    rhs[bi[ib]] = c*Zext[ib]

    M = sp.coo_matrix((np.concatenate(vv), (np.concatenate(rr), np.concatenate(cc))), shape=(N, N)).tocsc()
    sol = spla.splu(M).solve(rhs)
    Z = np.full((ny, nx), np.nan + 0j)
    Z[wet] = sol[:nz]
    # volume budget check:  Q_in = i sigma * sum(zeta * area)
    vb = sol[bi[ib]]
    Qin = np.sum(vb*H[0, ib]*A_E*coss[0, ib]*d)
    dV = 1j*sigma*np.sum(sol[:nz]*(A_E**2*cosc[wet]*d*d))
    return dict(Z=Z, budget_err=abs(Qin - dV)/max(abs(Qin), 1e-30), unknowns=N)


# ═══════════════════════════ checks ═══════════════════════════
def check_channel():
    """Non-rotating, constant-depth channel closed at one end vs exact 1D solution with Flather boundary."""
    res, ny, nx = 0.05, 80, 5
    lat_c = (np.arange(ny) + 0.5)*res; lon_c = np.arange(nx)*res
    wet = np.zeros((ny, nx), bool); wet[:, 1:4] = True
    h, r = 70.0, 5e-5
    B = make_B(wet, np.where(wet, h, 0.0), res, lon_c, lat_c, wet[0].copy()); B["R"] = np.where(wet, r, 0.0)
    dy = A_E*np.radians(res); L = ny*dy; y = (np.arange(ny) + 0.5)*dy; cw = np.sqrt(g_acc/h)
    worst = 0.0
    for T in (5.0, 8.0, 12.42, 18.0, 24.0):
        s = 2*np.pi/(T*3600)
        Zn = solve_tide(B, s, 1.0, coriolis=False)["Z"][:, 2]
        k = np.sqrt(s*(s - 1j*r)/(g_acc*h) + 0j)
        A0 = cw/(cw*np.cos(k*L) - g_acc*k*np.sin(k*L)/(1j*s + r))
        Za = A0*np.cos(k*(L - y))
        worst = max(worst, np.abs(Zn - Za).max()/np.abs(Za).max())
    return worst


def nearest_wet(B, lon, lat):
    LON, LAT = np.meshgrid(B["lon_c"], B["lat_c"])
    d2 = ((LON - lon)*np.cos(np.radians(lat)))**2 + (LAT - lat)**2
    d2[~B["wet"]] = np.inf
    j, i = np.unravel_index(np.argmin(d2), d2.shape)
    return j, i, 111.2*np.sqrt(d2[j, i])


def station_mean(Z, Bx, lon, lat, radius_km):
    """Complex mean of Z over the wet cells within radius_km of a point (robust against coastal gradients)."""
    LONg, LATg = np.meshgrid(Bx["lon_c"], Bx["lat_c"])
    dist = 111.2*np.hypot((LONg - lon)*np.cos(np.radians(lat)), LATg - lat)
    m = Bx["wet"] & (dist <= radius_km)
    if not m.any():
        j, i, _ = nearest_wet(Bx, lon, lat); return Z[j, i]
    return Z[m].mean()


def boundary_forcing(Bx, cons=None):
    """Complex external level per constituent (see docstring)."""
    out = {}
    for c, T in CONSTITUENTS.items():
        if cons and c not in cons:
            continue
        Ao, go_ = OBS[BOUNDARY_STATION][c]
        Zo = Ao/100.0*np.exp(-1j*np.radians(go_))
        kap = station_mean(solve_tide(Bx, 2*np.pi/(T*3600), 1.0)["Z"], Bx, *STATIONS[BOUNDARY_STATION], CAL_RADIUS_KM) if CALIBRATE_FORCING else 1.0
        out[c] = Zo/kap
    return out


def lag_deg(Z):
    return (-np.degrees(np.angle(Z))) % 360.0


def amphidromes(Z, B):
    """2x2-cell blocks around which the phase winds by 2*pi."""
    wet, res = B["wet"], B["res"]
    ph = np.angle(Z)
    ok = wet[:-1, :-1] & wet[:-1, 1:] & wet[1:, 1:] & wet[1:, :-1]
    dd = lambda a, b: np.angle(np.exp(1j*(b - a)))
    w = np.where(ok, dd(ph[:-1, :-1], ph[:-1, 1:]) + dd(ph[:-1, 1:], ph[1:, 1:]) + dd(ph[1:, 1:], ph[1:, :-1])
                 + dd(ph[1:, :-1], ph[:-1, :-1]), 0.0)
    jj, ii = np.nonzero(np.abs(w) > np.pi)
    return [(B["lon_c"][i] + res/2, B["lat_c"][j] + res/2, "counter-clockwise" if w[j, i] < 0 else "clockwise")
            for j, i in zip(jj, ii)]

title: Governing equations of incompressible fluids in non-inertial reference frames
text:
Navier-Stokes equations in inertial reference frame
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \\
  & \rho \frac{D \mathbf{u}}{D t} = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} \ ,
\end{aligned} \right.\]
with the stress tensor for an incompressible Newtonian fluid, \(\mathbb{T} = - p \mathbb{I} + \mathbb{S} = - p \mathbb{I} + 2 \mu \mathbb{D}\), and the deformation velocity tensor \(\mathbb{D} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \nabla \mathbf{u} + \nabla^T \mathbf{u} \right)\).
Relative kinematics
\[\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{r}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{r}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
  \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
  \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{a}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\alpha_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} + 2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
\end{aligned}\]
Navier stokes in the non-inertial reference frame.
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \\
  & \rho \frac{D \mathbf{v}}{D t} = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} - \rho \left\{ \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \boldsymbol\alpha_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r} + 2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r} \right\} \ ,
\end{aligned} \right.\]
with \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) the position and the velocity w.r.t. the origin of the non-inertial reference frame.






NoteIncompressibility constraint





Let \(\mathbf{u} := \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{P/Q}\), and \(\mathbf{v} := \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q}\). Then
\[\begin{aligned}
  \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r},t)
  & = \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{Q/O}(t) + \mathbf{v}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r},t) + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0}(t) \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \right) = \\
  & = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r},t) \ .
\end{aligned}\]
Here the argument of the fields is \(\mathbf{r}\)









NoteDivergence \(\ \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{r} \right)\), with \(\mathbf{a}\) independent from space





\[
  \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{r} \right)
    = \partial_i \left( \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j r_k \right)
    = \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j \delta_{ik} = \varepsilon_{iji} a_j \equiv 0 \ ,
\]
since the symbols \(\varepsilon_{ijk}\) with repeated indices are zero.









NoteChange of coordinates





Let \(\{ x^0, y^0, z^0 \}\) a set of Cartesian coordinates describing the points in space w.r.t. an inertial reference frame \((0)\). Let \(\{ x^1, y^1, z^1 \}\) a set of Cartsisan coordinates at rest w.r.t. the non-inertial reference frame \((1)\). The origin of the reference frame \(Q\) w.r.t. the origin of the reference frame \(O\) is in \(\mathbf{r}_{Q/O}\), its orientation is determined by the rotation tensor \(\mathbb{R}^{0\to1}\) transforming the vectors of the Carteisan basis \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i\) into the corresponding vectors of the Cartesian basis \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i\),
\[\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{1}_i = \mathbb{R}^{0\to1} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,\]
being \(\mathbb{R}^{0\to1} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k\), see Classical Mechanics: Kinematics: Rotations. For orthogonal bases, the transformation is immediately obtained with orthogonal projection of the vectors of the other bases,
\[\hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i = \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \left[ \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k  \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j \right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,\]
and thus \(\mathbb{R}^{0\to1} = \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k  \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j = R^{0\to1}_{kj} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j\), with \(R^{0\to1}_{kj} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j\). Using the transformation of the vectors of the bases, the transformation of the the components of the vectors immedately follows
\[\mathbf{w} = w^0_i \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i = w^0_i R^{0\to1}_{ik} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k = w^1_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \ ,\]
so that \(w^1_k = w^0_i R^{0\to1}_{ik}\), and \(w^0_i = w^1_k R^{0\to1}_{ik}\). Thus, the relative position of a point \(P\) w.r.t. \((0)\) can be written as
\[\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{r}_{P/O}
  & = \mathbf{r}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} = \\
  & = \left( r^0_{Q/O,i} + r^0_{P/Q,i} \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i = \\
  & = \left( r^0_{Q/O,i} + r^1_{P/Q,k} R^{0\to1}_{ik} \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,
\end{aligned}\]
This relation holds for every point \(P\), and thus the law of transformation of coordinates is
\[\begin{aligned}
  r^0_i & = r^0_{Q,i}(t) + R^{0\to1}_{ik}(t) \, r^1_k \\
  r^1_k & =  R^{0\to1}_{ik}(t) \left( r^0_i - r^0_{Q,i}(t) \right) \\
\end{aligned}\]
Thus, the derivative w.r.t. \(r_i^0\) reads
\[\partial^i_0 = \frac{\partial r^1_k}{\partial r^0_i} \partial^1_k = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \partial^1_k \ .\]
Differential operators.

Gradient of a scalar field
\[\nabla_0 f(\mathbf{r}_0) = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \partial^0_i f = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k R^{0\to1}_{ij} \partial^1_j f = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \partial^1_k f = \nabla_1 f(\mathbf{r}_1) \ ,\]
Divergence of a vector field
\[\nabla_0 \cdot \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0) = \partial^0_i w^0_i = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \partial^1_k \left( R^{0\to1}_{ij} w^1_j \right) = \delta_{jk} \partial^1_{k} w^1_j = \partial^1_k w^1_k = \nabla_1 \cdot \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .\]
Advection operator
\[\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \nabla_0 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0)
  & = a^0_i \partial^0_i w^0_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \\
  & = R^{0\to1}_{i \alpha} R^{0\to1}_{i \beta} R^{0\to1}_{k \gamma} R^{0\to1}_{k \delta} a^1_\alpha \partial^1_\beta w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\delta = \\
  & = a^1_\alpha \partial^1_\alpha w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\gamma = \\
  & = \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}_1) \cdot \nabla_1 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .
\end{aligned}\]
Laplacian of a vector field
\[\begin{aligned}
  \Delta_0 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0)
  & = \partial^0_i \partial^0_i w^0_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \\
  & = R^{0\to1}_{i \alpha} R^{0\to1}_{i \beta} R^{0\to1}_{k \gamma} R^{0\to1}_{k \delta} \partial^1_\alpha \partial^1_\beta w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\delta = \\
  & = \partial^1_\alpha \partial^1_\alpha w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\gamma = \\
  & = \Delta_1 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .
\end{aligned}\]

title: Governing equations of incompressible fluids in non-inertial reference frames
text:
Navier-Stokes equations in inertial reference frame
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0} \\
  & \rho \frac{D \mathbf{u}}{D t} = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} \ ,
\end{aligned} \right.\]
with the stress tensor for an incompressible Newtonian fluid, \(\mathbb{T} = - p \mathbb{I} + \mathbb{S} = - p \mathbb{I} + 2 \mu \mathbb{D}\), and the deformation velocity tensor \(\mathbb{D} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \nabla \mathbf{u} + \nabla^T \mathbf{u} \right)\).
Relative kinematics
\[\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{r}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{r}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
  \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
  \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{P/O} & = \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{a}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\alpha_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} + 2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \\
\end{aligned}\]
Navier stokes in the non-inertial reference frame.
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \\
  & \rho \frac{D \mathbf{v}}{D t} = \rho \mathbf{g} + \nabla \cdot \mathbb{T} - \rho \left\{ \mathbf{a}^{(0)}_{Q/O} + \boldsymbol\alpha_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r} + 2 \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{v} + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0} \times \mathbf{r} \right\} \ ,
\end{aligned} \right.\]
with \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) the position and the velocity w.r.t. the origin of the non-inertial reference frame.






NoteIncompressibility constraint





Let \(\mathbf{u} := \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{P/Q}\), and \(\mathbf{v} := \mathbf{v}^{(1)}_{P/Q}\). Then
\[\begin{aligned}
  \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{r},t)
  & = \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{v}^{(0)}_{Q/O}(t) + \mathbf{v}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r},t) + \boldsymbol\omega_{1/0}(t) \times \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} \right) = \\
  & = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{r},t) \ .
\end{aligned}\]
Here the argument of the fields is \(\mathbf{r}\)









NoteDivergence \(\ \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{r} \right)\), with \(\mathbf{a}\) independent from space





\[
  \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{r} \right)
    = \partial_i \left( \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j r_k \right)
    = \varepsilon_{ijk} a_j \delta_{ik} = \varepsilon_{iji} a_j \equiv 0 \ ,
\]
since the symbols \(\varepsilon_{ijk}\) with repeated indices are zero.









NoteChange of coordinates





Let \(\{ x^0, y^0, z^0 \}\) a set of Cartesian coordinates describing the points in space w.r.t. an inertial reference frame \((0)\). Let \(\{ x^1, y^1, z^1 \}\) a set of Cartsisan coordinates at rest w.r.t. the non-inertial reference frame \((1)\). The origin of the reference frame \(Q\) w.r.t. the origin of the reference frame \(O\) is in \(\mathbf{r}_{Q/O}\), its orientation is determined by the rotation tensor \(\mathbb{R}^{0\to1}\) transforming the vectors of the Carteisan basis \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i\) into the corresponding vectors of the Cartesian basis \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i\),
\[\hat{\mathbf{e}}^{1}_i = \mathbb{R}^{0\to1} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,\]
being \(\mathbb{R}^{0\to1} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k\), see Classical Mechanics: Kinematics: Rotations. For orthogonal bases, the transformation is immediately obtained with orthogonal projection of the vectors of the other bases,
\[\hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i = \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \left[ \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k  \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j \right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,\]
and thus \(\mathbb{R}^{0\to1} = \left( \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k  \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j = R^{0\to1}_{kj} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \otimes \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_j\), with \(R^{0\to1}_{kj} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_j\). Using the transformation of the vectors of the bases, the transformation of the the components of the vectors immedately follows
\[\mathbf{w} = w^0_i \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i = w^0_i R^{0\to1}_{ik} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k = w^1_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \ ,\]
so that \(w^1_k = w^0_i R^{0\to1}_{ik}\), and \(w^0_i = w^1_k R^{0\to1}_{ik}\). Thus, the relative position of a point \(P\) w.r.t. \((0)\) can be written as
\[\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{r}_{P/O}
  & = \mathbf{r}_{Q/O} + \mathbf{r}_{P/Q} = \\
  & = \left( r^0_{Q/O,i} + r^0_{P/Q,i} \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i = \\
  & = \left( r^0_{Q/O,i} + r^1_{P/Q,k} R^{0\to1}_{ik} \right) \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \ ,
\end{aligned}\]
This relation holds for every point \(P\), and thus the law of transformation of coordinates is
\[\begin{aligned}
  r^0_i & = r^0_{Q,i}(t) + R^{0\to1}_{ik}(t) \, r^1_k \\
  r^1_k & =  R^{0\to1}_{ik}(t) \left( r^0_i - r^0_{Q,i}(t) \right) \\
\end{aligned}\]
Thus, the derivative w.r.t. \(r_i^0\) reads
\[\partial^i_0 = \frac{\partial r^1_k}{\partial r^0_i} \partial^1_k = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \partial^1_k \ .\]
Differential operators.

Gradient of a scalar field
\[\nabla_0 f(\mathbf{r}_0) = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_i \partial^0_i f = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k R^{0\to1}_{ij} \partial^1_j f = \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_k \partial^1_k f = \nabla_1 f(\mathbf{r}_1) \ ,\]
Divergence of a vector field
\[\nabla_0 \cdot \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0) = \partial^0_i w^0_i = R^{0\to1}_{ik} \partial^1_k \left( R^{0\to1}_{ij} w^1_j \right) = \delta_{jk} \partial^1_{k} w^1_j = \partial^1_k w^1_k = \nabla_1 \cdot \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .\]
Advection operator
\[\begin{aligned}
  \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \nabla_0 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0)
  & = a^0_i \partial^0_i w^0_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \\
  & = R^{0\to1}_{i \alpha} R^{0\to1}_{i \beta} R^{0\to1}_{k \gamma} R^{0\to1}_{k \delta} a^1_\alpha \partial^1_\beta w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\delta = \\
  & = a^1_\alpha \partial^1_\alpha w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\gamma = \\
  & = \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}_1) \cdot \nabla_1 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .
\end{aligned}\]
Laplacian of a vector field
\[\begin{aligned}
  \Delta_0 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_0)
  & = \partial^0_i \partial^0_i w^0_k \hat{\mathbf{e}}^0_k = \\
  & = R^{0\to1}_{i \alpha} R^{0\to1}_{i \beta} R^{0\to1}_{k \gamma} R^{0\to1}_{k \delta} \partial^1_\alpha \partial^1_\beta w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\delta = \\
  & = \partial^1_\alpha \partial^1_\alpha w^1_\gamma \hat{\mathbf{e}}^1_\gamma = \\
  & = \Delta_1 \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{r}_1) \ .
\end{aligned}\]

title: Dynamics of a straight channel
text:
1 Governing equations
Shallow water equations are used here to model the dynamics of the water in the channel. Link






NoteShallow water equations






1.1 Non-linear equations in a multi-dimensional domain
In conservative form
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
& \partial_t \zeta + \nabla \cdot \left( \zeta \mathbf{u} \right) = 0 \\
& \partial_t \left( \zeta \mathbf{u} \right) + \nabla \cdot \left( \zeta \mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u} + \frac{g \zeta^2}{2} \mathbf{I} \right) = \mathbf{0} \ ,
\end{aligned}\right.\]
or in convective form
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
& \partial_t \zeta + \nabla \cdot \left( \zeta \mathbf{u} \right) = 0 \\
& \zeta \partial_t \mathbf{u} +  \zeta \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla  \mathbf{u} + g \zeta \nabla \zeta = \mathbf{0} \ ,
\end{aligned}\right.\]


1.2 Linearized equations in a 1-dimensional domain
The linearized equations around the reference state \((\zeta, u) = (h, 0)\) read
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
& \partial_t \zeta + h \partial_x u = 0 \\
& \partial_t u + g \partial_x \zeta = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\right.\]
In this model a linear friction contribution (\(r \ge 0\)) is introduced to the momentum equation
\[\partial_t u + g \partial_x \zeta + r u = 0 \ ,\]
adding a reactive term to the convection modeled in the hyperbolic system.


1.3 Wave equation, with dissipation
\[\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = \partial_{tt} \zeta + h \partial_{xt} u = \\
  & = \partial_{tt} \zeta - h \partial_x \left( g \partial_x \zeta + r u \right) =  \\
  & = \partial_{tt} \zeta - gh \partial_{xx} \zeta - h r \partial_x u = \\
  & = \partial_{tt} \zeta - gh \partial_{xx} \zeta + r \partial_t \zeta \ .
\end{aligned}\]

title: Dynamics of a straight channel
text:
2 Toy problem
The problem can be recast as a modified wave equation with dissipation
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \frac{1}{gh} \partial_{tt} \zeta - \partial_{xx} \zeta + \frac{r}{gh} \partial_t \zeta = 0 \\
  & \zeta(0,t) = Z f(t) \\
  & \partial_x \zeta(L,t) = 0
\end{aligned}\right.\]






NoteShallow water equations





The equations in the domain are supplied with boundary conditions. Convective form of the non-linear equation in 1-dimensional domain w.r.t. an inertial reference frame,
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
& \partial_t \zeta + \zeta \partial_x u + u \partial_x \zeta = 0 \\
& \partial_t u + u \partial_x u + g \partial_x \zeta = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\right.\]
Linearized equations. Around the reference condition \((\zeta_0, u_0) = (h, 0)\).
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
& \partial_t \zeta + h \partial_x u = 0 \\
& \partial_t u + g \partial_x \zeta = 0 \ .
\end{aligned}\right.\]
In the simulation a linear friction contribution (\(r \ge 0\)) is added to the momentum equation
\[\partial_t u + g \partial_x \zeta + r u = 0 \ ,\]
adding a reactive term to the convection modeled in the hyperbolic system.
Boundary conditions.
\[\begin{aligned}
  \zeta(0,t) & = Z f(t) \quad , \quad
  u(L,t) = 0
\end{aligned}\]
Since the second condition holds for all the time-steps then \(\partial_t u(L,t) = 0\), and linearized momentum equation implies \(\partial_x \zeta = - \frac{1}{g} \partial_t u\), then the second boundary conditions can be written as a function of \(\zeta\),
\[\partial_x \zeta( L, t) = 0 \ .\]
A wave equation for \(\zeta\) follows from the linearized hyperbolic system, so that the problem can be written as a function of \(\zeta(x,t)\) only
\[\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  & \frac{1}{gh} \partial_{tt} \zeta - \partial_{xx} \zeta = 0 \\
  & \zeta(0,t) = Z f(t) \\
  & \partial_x \zeta(L,t) = 0
\end{aligned}\right.\]
Modified wave equation for the system with friction.
\[\begin{aligned}
  0
  & = \partial_{tt} \zeta + h \partial_{xt} u = \\
  & = \partial_{tt} \zeta - h \partial_x \left( g \partial_x \zeta + r u \right) =  \\
  & = \partial_{tt} \zeta - gh \partial_{xx} \zeta - h r \partial_x u = \\
  & = \partial_{tt} \zeta - gh \partial_{xx} \zeta + r \partial_t \zeta \ .
\end{aligned}\]




2.1 Analytical solution of the problem, with series on natural modes
Ideal system. The solution of ideal problem - without dissipation - can be written as the sum of a homogeneous term and a series of natural modes,
\[\zeta(x,t) = \zeta_0(t) + \widetilde{\zeta}(x,t) = \zeta_0(t) + \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} f_n(x) g_n(t) \ ,\]
with the uniform function \(\zeta_0(t) = Z f(t)\) satisfying the boundary conditions, and working as a forcing for the linear combination of natural modes, with space shape
\[f_n(x) = \sin(k_n x) \ ,\]
with wave-vector \(k_n = \left( n - \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi}{L}\), and amplitudes \(g_n(t)\) satisfying the (infinite) decoupled system of ODEs
\[\ddot{g}_{n}(t) + \omega_n^2 g_{n}(t) = - \frac{2}{\left(n-\frac{1}{2}\right) \pi} Z \ddot{f}(t) \ ,\]
with \(\omega_n = c k_n = k_n \sqrt{gh}\).






NoteAnalytical solution of the ideal system, with series on natural modes





Analytical solution of the problem. The solution can be written as the sum of a uniform function (fast part, as it instantaneously adapts to the boundary condition), and the series of natural modes (that can be then separated into slow modes - whose dynamics is solved - and fast modes - that are either truncated, or whose contribution is statically recovered),
\[\zeta(x,t) = \zeta_0(t) + \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} f_n(x) g_n(t) = \zeta_0(t) + \widetilde{\zeta}(x,t) \ .\]
The uniform function identically satisfies the boundary condition in \(x = L\). In order to satisfy the boundary condition in \(x=0\) for \(\forall t\), \(\zeta_0(t) = Z f(t)\). This function doesn’t satisfy the wave equation, and thus it acts as a forcing contribution for the series of natural modes,
\[\frac{1}{c^2} \partial_{tt} \widetilde\zeta - \partial_{xx} \widetilde\zeta = - \frac{1}{c^2} \partial_{tt} \zeta_0 = - \frac{Z}{c^2} \ddot{f}(t) \ .\]
Natural modes are evaluated solving the homogeneous problem for \(\widetilde\zeta(x,t)\), using separation of variables,
\[- k_n^2 = \frac{f''_n(x)}{f_n(x)} \qquad \text{only if homogeneous} = \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\ddot{g}_n(t)}{g_n(t)} \]

applying boundary conditions to set constants of integration
\[f_n(x) = A_n \sin\left( k_n x \right) \ ,\]
with \(k_n = \left( n - \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi}{L}\).
then solving the inhomogeneous problem to evaluate the time coefficients of the natural modes, exploiting their orthogonality

\[\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} \left\{ \frac{1}{c^2} \ddot{g}_n(t)  + k_n^2 g_n(t)  \right\} \sin(k_n x) = - \frac{Z}{c^2} \ddot{f}(t) \ ,\]
Multiplying by \(\sin(k_m x)\) and integrating over \(x \in [0, L]\) provides the decoupled dynamical equations for the amplitude of the modes,
\[\ddot{g}_{n}(t) + \omega_n^2 g_{n}(t) = - \frac{2}{\left(n-\frac{1}{2}\right) \pi} Z \ddot{f}(t) \ ,\]
with \(\omega_n = c k_n\).









NoteDetails about Fourier expansion and orthogonality of Fourier base functions





\[\begin{aligned}
  \int_{x=0}^{L} \sin\left[ \left( n- \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi}{L} x \right] \sin\left[  \left( m - \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi}{L} x \right] \, dx
  & = \frac{1}{2} \int_{x=0}^{L} \left\{ \cos\left[ \left( n - m \right) \frac{\pi}{L} x \right] - \cos\left[  \left( n + m - 1 \right) \frac{\pi}{L} x \right] \right\} \, dx = \\
\end{aligned}\]
using
\[\cos(\alpha \mp \beta) = \cos \alpha \cos \beta \pm \sin \alpha \sin \beta\]
\[\sin \alpha \sin \beta = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \cos(\alpha - \beta) - \cos(\alpha + \beta) \right]\]
The factor \(n-m\) is equal to zero if \(m = n\), its cosine is equal to \(1\), and the integral over \(x \in [0,L]\) is equal to \(\frac{L}{2}\). If \(m \ne n\), then the integral is identically zero, since \(\frac{L}{\pi(n-m)} \left. \sin\left( (n-m) \frac{\pi x}{L} \right)\right|_{x=0}^{L} = 0\).
Since \(m,n \in \mathbb{N}^+\), the factor \(n+m-1\) is always positive, and the integral of the second term is identically zero, since \(\frac{L}{\pi(n+m-1)} \left. \sin\left( (n+m-1) \frac{\pi x}{L} \right)\right|_{x=0}^{L} = 0\).

\[\int_{x=0}^{L} \sin\left[  \left( m - \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi}{L} x \right] \, dx = - \frac{L}{\left( m - \frac{1}{2} \right) \pi} \left. \cos \left[ \left( m - \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi}{L} x \right]\right|_{x=0}^{L} = \frac{L}{\left( m - \frac{1}{2} \right) \pi} \ .\]



Dissipative system. The solution of the dissipative system can be formally written as the solution of the ideal system, with the amplitudes of the natural modes satisfying the (infinite) decoupled system of ODEs
\[\ddot{g}_{n}(t) + r \dot{g}_n(t) + \omega_n^2 g_{n}(t) = - \frac{2}{\left(n-\frac{1}{2}\right) \pi} Z \left( \ddot{f}(t) + r \dot{f}(t) \right) \ ,\]
with \(\omega_n = c k_n = k_n \sqrt{gh}\).






NoteAnalytical solution of the dissipative system, with series on natural modes





Analytical solution Sum of a uniform function and a series of natural modes. The uniform function \(\zeta_0(x,t) = Z f(t)\) satisfies the non-homogeneous boundary conditions. Thus, the PDE for the series of natural modes is the non-homogeneous wave equation
\[\frac{1}{c^2} \partial_{tt} \widetilde\zeta - \partial_{xx} \widetilde\zeta + \frac{r}{c^2} \partial_t \widetilde\zeta = - \frac{Z}{c^2} \left( \ddot{f} + r \dot{f} \right) \ .\]
Natural modes are computed using separation of variables, \(\widetilde\zeta(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} f_n(x) g_n(t)\),
\[0 = \ddot{g} f - c^2 f'' g + r \dot{g} f \ ,\]
and dividing by \(c^2 g f\), and separating on opposite sides of the equal sign the functions of \(x\) and \(t\)
\[-k_n^2 = \frac{f_n''}{f_n}  \qquad \text{only if homogeneous} = \frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\ddot{g}_n + r \dot{g}_n}{g_n} \ .\]
and prescribing homogeneous boundary conditions for \(\widetilde\zeta\), \(\widetilde\zeta(0,t) = 0\), \(\partial_x \zeta(L,t) = 0\) (this condition can be derived from the boundary condition on \(u(L,t)\) and the momentum equation), it follows
\[f_n(x) = A_n \sin(k_n x) \ ,\]
with \(k_n = \left( n - \frac{1}{2} \right) \frac{\pi}{L}\). Introducing the series of natural modes in the non-homogeneous wave equation
\[\sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} \left\{ \ddot{g}_{n} + r \dot{g}_{n} + \omega_n^2 g_{n} \right\} \sin(k_n x) = - Z \left( \ddot{f} + r \dot{f} \right) \ ,\]
with \(\omega_n = k_n c = k_n \sqrt{gh}\). Exploiting the orthogonality of the basis functions, the decoupled set of equations for the amplitude of the modes reads
\[\ddot{g}_n + r \dot{g}_n + \omega_n^2 g_n = - \frac{2 Z}{\left(n-\frac{1}{2}\right) \pi} \left( \ddot{f}(t) + r \dot{f}(t) \right) \ .\]





2.2 Height of the water at the head of the channel
\[
\zeta(L,t) = \zeta_0(t) + \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} g_n(t) (-1)^{n+1}
\]






NoteHeight of the water at the head of the channel





The height of the free surface of the water at the head of the bay in \(x = L\) is
\[\begin{aligned}
  \zeta(L,t)
  & = \zeta_0(t) + \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} g_n(t) \sin\left( k_n L \right) = \\
  & = \zeta_0(t) + \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} g_n(t) (-1)^{n+1} \ ,
\end{aligned}\]
since \(\sin(k_n L) = (-1)^{n+1}\).





Parameters and useful functions
"""
Unsteady tides and resonance  (Colab / Plotly)
==============================================
LEVEL 1  Quarter-wave bay (Bay-of-Fundy-like): analytic resonance curve, checked
         against a time-domain finite-difference solver.
"""

import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots
import plotly.io as pio

pio.renderers.default = "notebook_connected"

# ───────────────────────── constants (SI) ─────────────────────────
G     = 6.67430e-11
M_E   = 5.9722e24
M_m   = 7.342e22
a     = 6.371e6                      # Earth radius
R_EM  = 3.844e8
Omega = 7.2921159e-5                 # sidereal spin rate
w_orb = 2*np.pi/(27.321661*86400.0)  # orbital rate (sidereal month)
g     = G*M_E/a**2

# ───────────────────────── user parameters ─────────────────────────
# Level 1: bay open at x=0 (sea tide imposed), closed at x=L
BAY_L, BAY_H, BAY_R = 300e3, 70.0, 5e-5      # length [m], depth [m], linear friction [1/s]
EPS_DEG        = 23.44        # obliquity (spin axis vs orbit normal)
THETA10_DEG    = 0.0          # initial orbital phase of the Earth centre

eps, theta10 = np.radians(EPS_DEG), np.radians(THETA10_DEG)
A = 1.5*(M_m/M_E)*a**4/R_EM**3                  # tidal amplitude coefficient [m]

# ==============================================================================
# Useful functions
# ==============================================================================
#   zeta_t + h u_x = 0 ,  u_t = -g zeta_x - r u ,  zeta(0,t) = Z cos(w t),  u(L,t)=0
# Frequency domain (exp(-i w t)):  zeta(x) = Z cos(k(L-x))/cos(kL),  k^2 = w(w + i r)/(g h)
# Gain at the head = 1/|cos(kL)|  ->  resonance at kL = pi/2, i.e. T0 = 4L/sqrt(gh).
def k_complex(sigma, h, r):
    return np.sqrt(sigma*(sigma + 1j*r)/(g*h) + 0j)


def bay_gain_head(T_h, L, h, r):
    sigma = 2*np.pi/(np.asarray(T_h)*3600.0)
    return 1.0/np.abs(np.cos(k_complex(sigma, h, r)*L))


def bay_profile(x, T_h, L, h, r):
    k = k_complex(2*np.pi/(T_h*3600.0), h, r)
    return np.abs(np.cos(k*(L - x))/np.cos(k*L))


def simulate_bay(T_h, L, h, r, Zs=1.0, N=150, cfl=0.5):
    """Forward-backward staggered-grid solver; returns the gain at the head."""
    c = np.sqrt(g*h); dx = L/N; dt = cfl*dx/c
    T = T_h*3600.0; w = 2*np.pi/T
    t_end = 6*(2.0/r) + 8*T
    n = int(t_end/dt)
    zeta = np.zeros(N); u = np.zeros(N + 1)
    gdt, hdt, fr = g*dt/dx, h*dt/dx, 1.0/(1.0 + r*dt)
    head = np.empty(n)
    for s in range(n):
        t = (s + 1)*dt
        zeta -= hdt*(u[1:] - u[:-1])
        u[1:N] = (u[1:N] - gdt*(zeta[1:] - zeta[:-1]))*fr
        u[0] = (u[0] - 2*gdt*(zeta[0] - Zs*np.cos(w*t)))*fr      # sea level imposed at x = 0
        head[s] = zeta[-1]
    times = dt*np.arange(1, n + 1)
    m = times >= t_end - 4*T
    Mx = np.column_stack([np.cos(w*times[m]), np.sin(w*times[m]), np.ones(m.sum())])
    coef = np.linalg.lstsq(Mx, head[m], rcond=None)[0]
    return np.hypot(coef[0], coef[1])/Zs

3 Frequency response

3.1 Transfer function of the mode amplitude \(\ G_n(\omega)\)
The solution in Fourier domain of the equation ref provides the transfer function between the forcing at the boundary condition and the amplitude of the \(n^{\rm th}\) natural mode,
\[\frac{\hat{g}_{n}(\omega)}{\hat{f}(\omega)} := G_n(\omega) = - \frac{2 Z}{\left(n-\frac{1}{2}\right) \pi} \cdot \frac{-\omega^2 + i r \omega}{-\omega^2 + i r \omega + \omega_n^2}  \ .\]
In this section the frequency response is plotted in unusual Bode diagrams, as a function of the period of the harmonic function \(T = \frac{2 \pi}{\omega}\).






NoteTransfer function of the mode amplitude \(\ G_n(\omega)\)





Let \(f(t) = e^{i \omega t}\) the frequency response of the amplitude of the \(n^{\rm th}\) mode has (complex) amplitude
\[G_n(\omega) = - \frac{2 Z}{\left(n-\frac{1}{2}\right) \pi} \cdot \frac{-\omega^2 + i r \omega}{-\omega^2 + i r \omega + \omega_n^2}\]

3.2 Solution of the dissipative wave equation in frequency-space domain
The frequency response of the system can be evaluated solving the dissipative wave equation in frequency-space domain. The solution reads
\[\begin{aligned}
  \hat{\zeta}(x,\omega) = Z \hat{f}(\omega) \frac{\cos(k(L-x))}{\cos(k L)} \ ,
\end{aligned}\]
with \(k\) a complex wave number, s.t. \(k^2 =  \frac{\omega^2 - i \omega r}{c^2}\). But what’s the cosine of a complex argument? See the box below to find the answer and realize how the imaginary part introduce modulation due to dispersion.
The frequency response at the head of the channel obtained as truncated solution using the uniform function \(\zeta_0(x,t)\) and the first \(5\) natural modes is compared to the exact solution, showing good agreement and thus good convergence of the modal series - at least in the range of frequencies shown.






NoteSolution in Fourier domain of Helmholtz equation





Solving in frequency response the modified wave equation. The semi-Fourier transform of the function \(\zeta(x,t)\),
\[\hat{\zeta}(x,\omega) := \mathscr{F}\{ \zeta(x,t) \}(\omega) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} \int_{t=-\infty}^{+\infty} \zeta(x,t) e^{-i\omega t} \, dt \ ,\]
satisfies transformed modified homogeneous wave equation
\[0 = -\omega^2 \hat{\zeta} - c^2 \hat{\zeta}'' + i \omega r \hat{\zeta}  \quad \rightarrow \quad  \hat{\zeta}'' + \frac{\omega^2 - i \omega r}{c^2} \hat{\zeta} = 0 \ ,\]
being \(( \cdot )' = \partial_x \left( \cdot \right)|_\omega\), with boundary conditions
\[
  \hat{\zeta}(0, \omega) = Z \hat{f}(\omega) \qquad , \qquad
  \hat{\zeta}'(L, \omega) = 0 \ .
\]
The solution of the equation in frequency domain reads \(\hat{\zeta}(x,\omega) = A_1 e^{i k_1 x} + A_2 e^{i k_2 x}\), with \(k_{1,2}\) the solutions of the equation
\[k^2 = \frac{\omega^2 - i \omega r}{c^2} \ ,\]
with \(k_{1,2}(\omega) = |k(\omega)| e^{i \left( \phi(\omega) + \pi (n-1) \right)}\), with
\[|k(\omega)| = \dots \quad , \quad \phi(\omega) = \dots\]
The two solutions are opposite, \(k_2 = - k_1\), and thus the solution in the frequency domain reads
\[\hat{\zeta}(x,\omega) = A_1 e^{i k_1 x} + A_2 e^{-i k_1 x} \ .\]
Prescribing the boundary conditions.
\[\begin{aligned}
  Z \hat{f}(\omega) & = \hat{\zeta}(0,\omega) = A_1 + A_2 \\
  0 & = \hat{\zeta}'(L,\omega) = i k_1 \left( A_1 e^{i k_1 L} - A_2 e^{-i k_1 L} \right) \ ,
\end{aligned}\]
and thus \(A_2 = A_1 e^{i 2 k_1 L}\), and
\[Z \hat{f}(\omega) = A_1 \left( 1 + e^{i 2 k_1 L} \right)\]
\[\quad \rightarrow \quad
\left\{ \begin{aligned}
  A_1 & = \frac{Z \hat{f}(\omega)}{1 + e^{i 2 k_1 L}} \\
  A_2 & = \frac{Z \hat{f}(\omega)}{1 + e^{-i 2 k_1 L}}
\end{aligned}\right.\]
so that
\[\begin{aligned}
  \hat{\zeta}(x,\omega)
  & = A_1 e^{i k_1 x} + A_2 e^{-i k_1 x} = \\
  & = Z \hat{f}(\omega) \left\{ e^{-i k_1 L} \frac{e^{i k_1 x}}{e^{-i k_1 L} + e^{i k_1 L}} + e^{i k_1 L} \frac{e^{-i k_1 x}}{e^{-i k_1 L} + e^{i k_1 L}} \right\} \\
  & = Z \hat{f}(\omega) \left\{ \frac{ e^{i k_1 (x-L)} +  e^{-i k_1 (x-L)} }{e^{-i k_1 L} + e^{i k_1 L}} \right\} = \\
  & = Z \hat{f}(\omega) \frac{\cos(k_1(L-x))}{\cos(k_1 L)} \\
\end{aligned}\]









NoteCosine of a complex argument





In general \(k_1\) is complex, \(k_1 = k_r + i k_i\), so that
\[\begin{aligned}
  \cos(k_1 x)
  & = \frac{ e^{i k_r x} e^{-k_i x} + e^{-i k_r x} e^{k_i x}}{2} = \\
  & = \frac{[ \cos(k_r x) + i \sin(k_r x) ] e^{-k_i x} + [ \cos(k_r x) - i \sin(k_r x) ] e^{k_i x}}{2} = \\
  & = \cos(k_r x) \cosh(k_i x) - i \sin(k_r x) \sinh(k_i x) \ .
\end{aligned}\]
having exploited Euler relation and the definition of hyperbolic functions,
\[\begin{aligned}
  e^{i x} & = \cos(x) + i \sin(x) \\
  \cosh x & = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2} \\
  \sinh x & = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}
\end{aligned}\]









NoteHeight of the water at the head of the channel





Height at the head of the channel. The height at the head of the channel is \(\zeta(L,t)\). The frequency response follows
\[\hat{\zeta}(L, \omega) = Z \hat{f}(\omega) \frac{1}{\cos(k_1 L)} \ ,\]
with the transfer function
\[G(L, \omega) = \frac{1}{\cos(k_1 L)} = \frac{1}{\cos(k_r L) \cosh(k_i L) - i \sin(k_r L) \sinh(k_i L)}\]

title: Natural modes in structures
text: This post tries to answer a narrow question I’ve found on Physics SE, mainly about some doubts the OP1 had about standing waves — or natural or proper modes of vibration —, their definition and the role of boundary conditions in the differential problem, and response to external forcing arising from the YouTube video, Standing Waves Parti I: Demonstration, by James Dann, Ph.D.

title: Natural modes in structures
text:
Natural modes
Many structural problems are governed by a differential problem, whose discret(ized) counterpart is a second order dynamical system,
\[\mathbf{M} \ddot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{C} \dot{\mathbf{u}} + \mathbf{K} \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{f} \ ,\]
supplied with the proper conditions on the state \(\mathbf{u}(t)\), like initial values of the function and its first derivative for Cauchy problems (or initial value problems),


Remarks


This is a linear problem, and its solution can be written as a linear combination of a set of solutions
Proper modes: a basis for the non-trivial solution of the homogenous problem, i.e. the response of the system to a free system with no external forcing, to a non-zero initial condition
Mass matrix \(\mathbf{M}\) and stiffness matrix \(\mathbf{K}\) are symmetric, if dynamical equations are derived with a Lagrangian approach. Here a proof for rigid-body mechanical systems.
If no rigid degree of freedom exists, stiffness matrix is definite positive. If \(n_r\) independent degrees of freedom exists, stiffness matrix is semi-definite positive with a kernel of dimension \(n_r\) (or it’s \(n_r\) times singular).
If there’s no degree of freedom associated with zero-inertia, mass matrix is definite positive. Independent d.o.f.s with zero-inertia are usually associated with algebraic constraints: if corresponding d.o.f.s are not expressed as a function of the other d.o.f.s, mass matrix is semi-definite positive (with kernel of dimension \(n_c\), whose elements are the mass-less d.o.f.s; or it’s \(n_c\) times singular), and the governing equations can be written as a system of DAEs (dynamical-algebraic equations).
The modes of an undamped system, \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{0}\), simultaneously diagonalize mass and stiffness matrices. As a consequence of matrix symmetry, it’s easy to prove that modes are mutually orthogonal through mass and stiffness matrices
\[\begin{aligned}
   \mathbf{u}_i^T \mathbf{M} \mathbf{u}_j & = m_i \delta_{ij} & \text{(no sum)} \\
   \mathbf{u}_i^T \mathbf{K} \mathbf{u}_j & = k_i \delta_{ij} & \text{(no sum)} \\
\end{aligned}\]
Mechanical systems with no dampers usually have small damping. This condition is treated in detail here. In the small-damping regime, damping matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) can be treated as a small perturbation of the undamped system, and two assumptions emerge as reasonable assumptions:

\(\mathbf{C}\) is semi-definite positive
modal basis \(\{ \hat{\mathbf{u}}_i \}\) makes the damping matrix \(\mathbf{C}\) diagonal
\[\hat{\mathbf{u}}^T_i \mathbf{C} \hat{\mathbf{u}}_j = c_i \delta_{ij} \ ,\]
as well.

If many eigenvectors exist with the same eigenvalue, it’s possible to define an orthogonal basis of that subspace
